explanations.answer: Bring them to Jerusalem as prisoners
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The letters are so that if Saul finds any men or women of the Way, he can “bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:2). Damascus is where he'd find them, and Jerusalem is where they'd be taken. So the whole trip is built around one goal.

explanations.answer: Drive them out of the city
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Nothing in the text has Saul driving anyone out of Damascus. He plans to “bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:2). Prisoners get brought somewhere, not sent away.

explanations.answer: Put them on trial in Damascus
explanations.explanation: Close, but a trial isn't in the text. Saul's plan is to “bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:2). The verse doesn't mention a trial in either city. Damascus is where he'd find them, and Jerusalem is where they'd go.

I see why that might sound right, since Saul gets most of the attention here. But the text says he's after “any men or women belonging to the Way” (Acts 9:2). The women are in those letters too. I think this is a heavy part to read, so I'll say it plainly and keep moving.
Yes, friend. Verse 2 says “any men or women belonging to the Way” (Acts 9:2). It's both. This is a heavy part of the story, so I'll set the jokes down for a minute.

That's it, baker. Saul asks, “Who are You, Lord?” and the answer comes right back: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He replied (Acts 9:5). No hints, no guessing game. Saul asks, and Jesus gives His own name.

Not this time, friend. The voice answers Saul's question Himself: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He replied (Acts 9:5). Gabriel isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. When the speaker hands you His own name, there's nothing left to guess.
Elijah isn't in this passage, friend. Saul asks, “Who are You, Lord?” and gets his answer: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He replied (Acts 9:5). The voice says who He is. That settles it.

explanations.answer: He will be told what he must do
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Jesus says, “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do” (Acts 9:6). Saul set out with a plan in his letters (Acts 9:2). Now he's heading into the city to be told what he must do.

explanations.answer: He will meet the high priest there
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The high priest is who Saul went to for his letters (Acts 9:1-2), but Jesus never says Saul will meet him in the city. What Jesus says is that Saul will be told what he must do (Acts 9:6). That's the whole promise for that city.

explanations.answer: He will be put on trial there
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't mention a trial, friend. He says Saul will be told what he must do (Acts 9:6). Saul left with letters about bringing others in as prisoners (Acts 9:2), but nothing in this verse puts him on trial. What waits in the city is instructions.

That's a keeper, baker. The men traveling with Saul “stood there speechless” (Acts 9:7). They heard the voice but did not see anyone (Acts 9:7). I'd go quiet too, and quiet is not something I do easily.
Weeping isn't in the text, friend. The men “stood there speechless” (Acts 9:7). They heard the voice but did not see anyone. Standing still and saying nothing is what the verse gives us.

Rejoicing doesn't show up in this verse, baker. What it says is that the men “stood there speechless” (Acts 9:7). I think hearing a voice with nobody in sight would do that to a person. The text says they heard the voice but did not see anyone.

Yes, baker. Saul got up from the ground, but he couldn't see a thing, so “they led him by the hand into Damascus” (Acts 8:8 is not it, it's Acts 9:8). He's on his own feet, with someone's hand guiding him. A man who came to bring others in as prisoners is now being walked in by the hand himself.
No mat in this story, friend. “Saul got up from the ground” (Acts 9:8), so he was on his feet. Then they led him by the hand into Damascus (Acts 9:8). It's a hand, not a stretcher.

A donkey would've been a comfy ride, but the text doesn't mention one. Saul got up from the ground, and they led him by the hand into Damascus (Acts 9:8). So he walked, with a hand guiding him. No saddle needed, just a steady grip.

True, baker. For three days he was without sight, and “he did not eat or drink anything” (Acts 9:9). That's three full days with no food and no water. I can't make it three hours without checking on my ovens.

The text says otherwise, friend. For three days Saul was without sight, and “he did not eat or drink anything” (Acts 9:9). That means no food and no water for those days. I think that was a quiet, heavy stretch.

explanations.answer: A man from Tarsus named Saul
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The Lord tells Ananias to go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for “a man from Tarsus named Saul” (Acts 9:11). Street, house and name, all in one sentence. I wish every set of directions I've ever gotten were that clear.

explanations.answer: A man from Cyprus named Barnabas
explanations.explanation: Barnabas is a fine name, friend, but he isn't in this passage. The Lord says to ask for “a man from Tarsus named Saul” (Acts 9:11). The name on the list is Saul, and the text says he is praying. So Ananias is looking for Saul.

explanations.answer: A man from Cyrene named Simon
explanations.explanation: Simon from Cyrene isn't in this passage, friend. The Lord says to ask for “a man from Tarsus named Saul” (Acts 9:11). The address is Judas's house on Straight Street. The name to ask for is Saul.

Right, baker. The Lord says Saul “has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight” (Acts 9:12). So both men get a vision in this stretch (Acts 9:10, 9:12). Two men, two visions, one very specific appointment.

Not in the text, friend. What Saul sees in the vision is Ananias placing his hands on him to restore his sight (Acts 9:12). Reading Scripture isn't mentioned there. The vision is about sight, and Saul can't see a thing right now (Acts 9:8).

Leading him home isn't in the vision, baker. The Lord says Saul saw Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight (Acts 9:12). The hand-leading already happened back in verse 8, when Saul's companions led him into Damascus (Acts 9:8). This vision is about his sight.

True, baker. Ananias says Saul is there with “authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name” (Acts 9:14). He's speaking straight to the Lord, and he doesn't hold back. I think Ananias is nervous, and that makes sense to me.

Actually, that's in there, friend. Ananias tells the Lord that Saul is here with “authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name” (Acts 9:14). He says it right after telling about the harm done in Jerusalem (Acts 9:13). It's his second point, and it's a big one.

You got it, baker. The Lord says Saul will carry His name “before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel” (Acts 9:15). Gentiles means the nations outside Israel. A man who showed up with letters is now hearing about kings.

Not what the Lord says, friend. His list is “the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel” (Acts 9:15). The chief priests do show up in this passage, but only as the ones who gave Saul authority (Acts 9:14). They aren't on the list of who he'll carry the name to.

Not on the Lord's list, baker. He names the Gentiles and their kings, and the people of Israel (Acts 9:15). The disciples in Damascus show up later, when Saul spends several days with them (Acts 9:19). Different part of the story.
Not quite, friend. The Lord says, “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name” (Acts 9:16). Suffering is part of what He says is coming. It's a heavy line, and I won't joke on top of it.

Yes, baker. The Lord says, “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name” (Acts 9:16). That line comes right after He calls Saul His chosen instrument (Acts 9:15). It's a heavy one, so I'll set the jokes down for this card.

That's it, baker. Ananias says, “Brother Saul” (Acts 9:17). A few verses earlier, he was telling the Lord about all the harm this man had done (Acts 9:13). Now he has his hands on Saul and calls him brother. That's a lot of ground to cover in four verses.
Master isn't what Ananias says, friend. The text has him say, “Brother Saul” (Acts 9:17). He says it as he places his hands on him. Brother is the word the verse gives.

Teacher is a fine word, but it's not what Ananias says. He says, “Brother Saul” (Acts 9:17). Remember, Ananias had heard about the harm Saul had done (Acts 9:13), so that greeting stands out. Brother is the word in the text.

Not in this story, friend. The text says, “At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored” (Acts 9:18). At that instant means no waiting around. No timer needed on this one.

Right, baker. It's instant: “At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored” (Acts 9:18). Notice the text says “something like scales,” so it's a comparison. After three days without sight (Acts 9:9), it comes back in a moment.
True, baker. Verse 18 says Saul “got up and was baptized” (Acts 9:18). It's the same verse where his sight comes back. Sight restored, up on his feet, baptized, all in one verse.
It does happen, friend. Once his sight is restored, Saul “got up and was baptized” (Acts 9:18). That's the very same verse. After that, he takes some food and regains his strength (Acts 9:19).

That's right, baker. Saul spent several days “with the disciples in Damascus” (Acts 9:19). That word, disciples, showed up back in verse 1 too (Acts 9:1). I can't tell you how those days went, because the text doesn't say.

Pharisees aren't mentioned in this passage, friend. The text says Saul spent several days “with the disciples in Damascus” (Acts 9:19). Disciples is the word the verse uses. That's where he spends those days.
Elders don't appear in this passage, baker. The verse says he spent several days “with the disciples in Damascus” (Acts 9:19). The word to look for is disciples. That's the group the text names.
